blocks.text: The coming Day has sharply contrasting effects: arrogant evildoers are consumed like dry stubble, while those who fear Jehovah’s name receive healing, freedom, and vindication. The “sun of righteousness” is a solar metaphor for that restoration; identifying it with a particular later person goes beyond the metaphor itself and belongs to the passage’s later reception.

The final commands join remembrance and expectation. Israel is told to remember the Torah of Moses—its statutes and ordinances given at Horeb—and is promised Elijah before the great and fearsome Day. Elijah’s work is described as turning parents and children toward one another. By ending with Moses and Elijah, the chapter brings Torah and prophecy together; this arrangement may also reflect the editorial shaping of Malachi and the wider collection of the Twelve.

sections.title: The Coming Day and the Book’s Conclusion

blocks.text: The reconciliation of parents and children belongs to Malachi’s own Persian-period setting, shaped by temple, kinship, agrarian, and covenant disputes. Any modern application should therefore distinguish those ancient institutions and relationships from later ones rather than assuming that the social settings are identical.
